problem: The lead says 'energy in equals energy out plus shaft work', which leaves out heat crossing the boundary and hides the case where shaft work enters (a compressor). A student can read it as Q = W_s, the very mistake the chapter later warns against.
fix: Say: energy in (with the incoming mass, plus any heat added) equals energy out (with the outgoing mass, plus any heat lost, plus shaft work done by the control volume), all as rates in kW.

problem: 'The two push works combine with u into enthalpy' suggests the inlet and outlet Pv are netted first and then added to u. In fact each stream forms its own enthalpy from its own pressure and specific volume.
fix: Say: at the inlet the upstream fluid does P1v1 per kg on the stream, so the energy it brings in is u1 + P1v1; at the outlet the control volume does P2v2 per kg on the surroundings, so the energy the stream takes out is u2 + P2v2. Writing h = u + Pv for each stream packs u and Pv into one property.

problem: 'Q − W_s equals the net energy carried by the flow' is vague. The right side is the energy carried out by the flow minus the energy carried in.
fix: Say: Q − W_s per unit mass equals the energy the outgoing stream carries away minus the energy the incoming stream brings in, counting h + V²/2 + gz for each stream.

problem: P1v1 = 1000 kJ/kg is not a realistic flow-work value for steam; for steam it is typically a few tens to a few hundred kJ/kg even at high pressure. The arithmetic of the answer is correct, but the numbers mislead a student about the size of Pv.
fix: Use realistic values, for example P1v1 = 300 kJ/kg at inlet and P2v2 = 60 kJ/kg at outlet, so the work is too low by 240 kJ/kg for each kg flowing. The reasoning and sign stay the same.
